sections.name: Reasoning in Humanities and Social Sciences
Reasoning in Biological, Physical and Chemical Sciences

questions.stem: A study finds that towns with more ice-cream shops also have higher rates of sunburn. A columnist concludes that ice-cream shops cause sunburn. What is the main flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: The sample size of towns studied was too small to be meaningful.
It mistakes a correlation for a causal relationship, ignoring a common cause (hot, sunny weather).
It assumes ice-cream shops are evenly distributed across all towns.
It fails to define what counts as an "ice-cream shop".

questions.explanation: Both variables (ice-cream sales and sunburn) rise together because of a third factor — hot, sunny weather — which drives both. Neither causes the other.
questions.principle_title: Correlation is not causation
questions.principle_explanation: Two things moving together (correlating) does not mean one causes the other. Always ask: could a third, hidden variable be driving both? GAMSAT Section I loves burying this pattern in social-science stimulus about health, crime, education or the economy.
questions.memory_tip: Picture a puppeteer ("the third variable") standing behind two puppets (ice-cream sales and sunburn), pulling both their strings at once — the puppets never touch each other directly. Whenever two things move together, go looking for the puppeteer.
questions.real_world_application: This is exactly the reasoning error behind decades of shaky health journalism — e.g. early claims that coffee "causes" heart disease, when confounders like smoking or stress were doing the real work. Any time you read "X is linked to Y", pause and ask what else might explain both.

questions.stem: "To be eligible for the scholarship, an applicant must have a GPA above 3.5." A student has a GPA of 3.8 but was rejected for the scholarship. Which statement is best supported?

options.text: The rule about GPA must be false.
A GPA above 3.5 is necessary but was not stated to be sufficient, so other criteria may also apply.
The student's GPA was calculated incorrectly.
The scholarship committee broke its own rule.

questions.explanation: The original statement only establishes GPA as a minimum requirement (necessary), not as a guarantee of selection (sufficient). Rejection despite meeting the minimum is fully consistent with other unstated criteria existing.
questions.principle_title: Necessary vs sufficient conditions
questions.principle_explanation: A necessary condition must be true for an outcome to happen ("you must have X"). A sufficient condition guarantees the outcome on its own ("having X is enough"). Confusing the two is one of the most common traps in GAMSAT Section I logic questions.
questions.memory_tip: N is a bouncer at the door: no ticket, no entry — but even with a ticket you might still be turned away for other reasons. S is a golden ticket that guarantees you get in, no questions asked. "Necessary = No entry without it, Sufficient = Ships you straight through."
questions.real_world_application: University admissions work this way: meeting the minimum GPA is necessary to be considered, but plenty of qualified applicants are still rejected because of other unstated criteria like references or fit. Spotting this distinction stops you from over- or under-reacting to a single requirement.

questions.stem: "We should build the new hospital downtown because that is where most people already work." What unstated assumption does this argument rely on?

options.text: Hospitals should be located near where people work rather than where they live.
Downtown land is cheaper than land elsewhere.
Most people who need the hospital will be at work when they need it.
The current hospital is poorly located.

questions.explanation: The argument jumps straight from "people work downtown" to "the hospital should be downtown" without ever stating why proximity to work (rather than home, transport links, etc.) is the relevant factor — that's the hidden premise doing the real work.
questions.principle_title: Finding the unstated assumption
questions.principle_explanation: Arguments often skip a step that feels "obvious" to the writer. To find it, ask: "what extra premise would I need to add to make this argument's conclusion actually follow from its stated evidence?" That missing premise is the assumption.
questions.memory_tip: Picture the argument as a rope bridge with one plank missing. The unstated assumption is that missing plank — ask "what would I need to nail down to stop this argument collapsing?"
questions.real_world_application: Public policy debates run on unstated assumptions constantly — "we should cut taxes because it grows the economy" hides an assumption about how people actually respond to tax changes. Naming the hidden assumption is usually the fastest way to find the weak point in a political argument.

questions.stem: "Naturally, the committee — in its infinite wisdom — decided the one thing nobody had asked for." The tone of this sentence is best described as:

options.text: Neutral and informative
Sincerely admiring
Sarcastic and critical
Fearful and anxious

questions.explanation: Phrases like "in its infinite wisdom" paired with "the one thing nobody had asked for" is verbal irony — praise-shaped words used to mock, signalling sarcasm and disapproval.
questions.principle_title: Reading tone through word choice, not just content
questions.principle_explanation: Tone lives in connotation, exaggeration and irony as much as in literal meaning. When praise is paired with a clearly negative outcome, that mismatch is usually sarcasm. Always check whether the literal words and the implied attitude actually match.
questions.memory_tip: The "sour candy" test: sugary-sweet words wrapped around a sour outcome (praise paired with a bad result) is the taste-test for sarcasm.
questions.real_world_application: Recognising sarcasm through word choice, not just content, is exactly the skill you need to read online reviews, satire, or a colleague's "sure, great idea" in a meeting without taking it at face value.

questions.stem: A passage opens by stating that public libraries are "the last truly free public space," then spends three paragraphs describing free wifi, warm shelter, and no obligation to buy anything. What is the main idea, and what are the paragraphs?

options.text: Main idea: libraries have wifi. Supporting detail: they are free public spaces.
Main idea: libraries are a uniquely unconditional public space. Supporting details: specific free, no-obligation features that illustrate this.
Main idea and supporting detail are the same thing here.
The passage has no identifiable main idea.

questions.explanation: The opening sentence is the claim (main idea); everything after it is evidence supporting that specific claim, not separate ideas of equal weight.
questions.principle_title: Main idea vs supporting detail
questions.principle_explanation: The main idea is the claim the whole passage serves; supporting details are the specific evidence, examples or reasons offered for that claim. A quick test: could you delete this sentence and still have the passage's core point survive? If yes, it's a detail, not the main idea.
questions.memory_tip: Trunk and branches: the main idea is the tree trunk holding everything up; supporting details are branches growing off it. Saw off a branch and the trunk still stands — that's the "delete it" test.
questions.real_world_application: Skimming a scientific abstract or a news article efficiently means finding the one main-idea sentence first, then treating everything else as evidence for it — this is how experienced readers get through dense material fast without missing the point.

questions.stem: "After the factory closed, the town's population fell by a third within five years." Which of the following is a valid inference (not just a restatement) of this sentence?

options.text: The factory closed.
The town's population fell by a third.
The factory was likely a major source of local employment or economic activity.
Five years passed.

questions.explanation: Options A, B and D simply repeat facts already given. Option C draws a new, reasonable conclusion from those facts — that the factory mattered economically to the town — without being stated outright.
questions.principle_title: Inference goes beyond the text; restatement stays inside it
questions.principle_explanation: An inference is a new claim you are justified in believing given the stimulus, even though the passage never says it directly. A restatement just repeats what's already written in different words. GAMSAT loves offering a restatement as a trap answer next to the real inference.
questions.memory_tip: Old news vs new news: restatement is old news said again in different words; inference is a genuinely new headline you're justified in printing based on the old news.
questions.real_world_application: Doctors do this constantly when reading patient notes: "chest pain and shortness of breath after climbing stairs" is data; "possible exertional angina" is an inference built on it. Confusing the two in clinical reasoning is a genuine patient-safety issue.

questions.stem: "All fish live in water. A dolphin lives in water. Therefore, a dolphin is a fish." This argument is:

options.text: Valid, because the conclusion follows the premises.
Invalid, because the premises do not logically guarantee the conclusion, even though the first premise is true.
Valid, because dolphins really do live in water.
Invalid, because "all fish live in water" is false.

questions.explanation: This is the classic "affirming the consequent" error: living in water doesn't make something a fish. The structure is logically broken regardless of whether the individual facts are true.
questions.principle_title: Validity is about structure, not the truth of individual facts
questions.principle_explanation: An argument can have true premises and still be logically invalid if the conclusion doesn't actually follow from them. Judge the argument's structure separately from whether you happen to agree with its claims.
questions.memory_tip: The cookie-cutter rule: validity is about the shape of the cutter (the logical structure), not the flavour of the dough (whether the individual facts are true).
questions.real_world_application: Legal arguments are judged the same way — a contract clause can be validly reasoned from its premises and still be unenforceable if one of those premises turns out to be false. Separating structure from truth is core to how lawyers and judges evaluate arguments.

questions.stem: Person A: "We should add a bike lane on Main Street to improve cyclist safety." Person B: "So you want to ban all cars from the city? That would destroy local businesses." Person B's response is an example of:

options.text: A straw man — misrepresenting A's modest proposal as an extreme one, then attacking that instead.
A valid counterargument to A's claim.
An appeal to authority.
A necessary clarification of A's position.

questions.explanation: A asked for one bike lane; B responded to "banning all cars," a much more extreme position A never took. Attacking the exaggerated version is easier than engaging with the real argument — that's the straw man.
questions.principle_title: The straw man fallacy
questions.principle_explanation: A straw man fallacy replaces someone's actual argument with a weaker, more extreme version, then knocks that down instead. Watch for a gap between what was actually claimed and what the response is arguing against.
questions.memory_tip: Picture a literal straw man propped up in a field — easy to knock down because nobody built it to withstand a punch. If the position being attacked feels oddly weak or extreme, check whether it's really a straw man standing in for the real argument.
questions.real_world_application: Political debates and social media arguments run on straw-manning constantly — replying to "we should regulate this industry more" with "so you want to ban all businesses?" Spotting the gap between the real claim and the exaggerated one is essential for following any contentious debate honestly.

questions.stem: "Either we cut the arts budget completely, or the school will go bankrupt." This statement is an example of:

options.text: A false dilemma — presenting only two extreme options when other possibilities (partial cuts, other savings) exist.
A sound cost-benefit analysis.
An appeal to emotion.
A circular argument.

questions.explanation: The statement ignores every middle-ground option — partial cuts, finding savings elsewhere, extra fundraising — and forces a choice between two extremes.
questions.principle_title: False dilemma (false dichotomy)
questions.principle_explanation: A false dilemma presents only two options as if they were the only possibilities, when in reality a range of options exists. Whenever you see "either... or..." phrasing in a persuasive passage, check whether a middle ground has been silently excluded.
questions.memory_tip: "Door number three": whenever an argument offers only two doors ("either... or..."), your job is to go looking for the door hiding just out of sight.
questions.real_world_application: Ultimatum-style pitches ("invest now or miss out forever") are usually false dilemmas engineered to rush a decision. Recognising the hidden middle ground is a core defence against high-pressure sales and political messaging alike.

questions.stem: "You can't trust her opinion on the new tax policy — she's never even run a business." This is best described as:

options.text: A relevant critique of her expertise on the specific topic.
An ad hominem attack, dismissing the argument by attacking the arguer rather than addressing the policy itself.
A logically valid deduction.
An appeal to popularity.

questions.explanation: It rejects the claim based on who is making it (their background) rather than examining the content of the tax policy argument itself.
questions.principle_title: Ad hominem: attacking the person, not the argument
questions.principle_explanation: An ad hominem dismisses a claim by criticising the person making it instead of engaging with their reasoning. Note: pointing out genuine, relevant lack of expertise can sometimes be legitimate context — the fallacy is using it to avoid the argument's substance entirely.
questions.memory_tip: "Play the ball, not the man" — a sports commentary phrase for fouls. If a response attacks the player instead of the ball (the argument), it's an ad hominem foul.
questions.real_world_application: You'll see this in every comment section: dismissing a scientist's climate data by pointing out they once worked for an oil company, instead of engaging with the data itself. It's a shortcut that feels satisfying but tells you nothing about whether the claim is true.

questions.stem: "This law is just because it is the law, and the law defines what is just." This statement demonstrates:

options.text: Circular reasoning — the conclusion is just a restatement of the premise, offering no independent support.
A hasty generalisation.
A slippery slope.
An appeal to tradition.

questions.explanation: The claim "this law is just" is defended by "the law defines justice" — which just assumes the very point being argued for, going in a circle rather than providing outside evidence.
questions.principle_title: Circular reasoning (begging the question)
questions.principle_explanation: Circular reasoning uses the conclusion (in disguise) as one of its own premises. Test for it by asking: "if I strip away the rewording, is the 'evidence' actually just the conclusion said a different way?"
questions.memory_tip: Merry-go-round: circular reasoning takes you for a ride that ends exactly where it started. If you can hop off at the "because" and land right back at the original claim, it's circular.
questions.real_world_application: Company policies sometimes get defended this way — "this is our process because it's how we've always done it" — which sounds like a reason but is really just the practice justifying itself. Spotting circularity helps you push for a policy's actual justification.

questions.stem: "Running a country is just like running a household budget — you can't spend more than you earn." What is the main weakness of this analogy?

options.text: Households never have any debt.
It ignores key disanalogies: a country can issue its own currency, borrow across generations, and influence its own income (tax/GDP) in ways a household cannot.
Households and countries both have budgets, so the analogy is actually perfect.
Governments never create budgets.

questions.explanation: Analogies persuade by similarity, but break down where the two things being compared differ in relevant ways. National economies have monetary tools (currency issuance, taxation, long-horizon borrowing) with no household equivalent.
questions.principle_title: Evaluating analogies by their disanalogies
questions.principle_explanation: An analogy is only as strong as the relevant similarities between the two things compared. To test one, actively look for a "disanalogy" — a relevant way the two cases differ that undermines the comparison.
questions.memory_tip: "Spot the odd sock": analogies work by matching pairs, so actively hunt for the one sock (the relevant difference, or disanalogy) that doesn't match its partner.
questions.real_world_application: Business strategy is full of shaky analogies ("we should run our startup like a special forces unit") — useful for one or two features but breaking down everywhere else. Testing an analogy by hunting its disanalogies is how good strategists avoid importing the wrong lessons.

questions.stem: A journalist interviews five people leaving a luxury car dealership and concludes "most people in this city are wealthy." The main problem with this conclusion is:

options.text: Five people is an unbiased, representative sample of the city.
The sample is both too small and drawn from a location (a luxury dealership) that is not representative of the general population.
The journalist should have asked ten people instead of five.
Wealth cannot be measured through interviews.

questions.explanation: Beyond the small sample size, the real problem is selection bias — people at a luxury dealership are far more likely to be wealthy than the city's population as a whole.
questions.principle_title: Hasty generalisation and sample bias
questions.principle_explanation: A conclusion about a whole population needs a sample that actually represents that population. Watch for two separate issues: sample size (too small to be reliable) and sample bias (drawn from an unrepresentative subgroup) — GAMSAT often tests whether you can tell these apart.
questions.memory_tip: Check both SIZE and SOURCE: a shaky sample can fail because it's too SIZE-small, drawn from the wrong SOURCE (a biased subgroup), or both — GAMSAT often hides one while flaunting the other.
questions.real_world_application: Market research gets this wrong constantly — surveying only existing customers about a new feature and concluding "everyone wants this" ignores that the sample is entirely people who already like the product. Sample-bias spotting is the first skill taught in intro statistics for exactly this reason.

questions.stem: "This diet must be effective — a famous actor recommended it on social media." Why is this reasoning weak?

options.text: Actors are always wrong about nutrition.
The person's fame is unrelated to relevant expertise (nutritional science), so their endorsement is not good evidence of effectiveness.
Social media posts are always false.
The diet has never been tried by anyone else.

questions.explanation: An appeal to authority is only strong when the "authority" has genuine, relevant expertise. Fame in acting says nothing about nutritional science.
questions.principle_title: Appeal to (irrelevant) authority
questions.principle_explanation: Citing an authority is a legitimate part of reasoning only when that authority has real expertise in the specific relevant field. When the credential doesn't match the claim, the appeal to authority is a fallacy, not evidence.
questions.memory_tip: Picture a celebrity chef being asked to fix your car engine: fame is a real credential, just filed under the wrong field for the claim being made — "right fame, wrong field."
questions.real_world_application: Supplement and skincare marketing leans on this daily — a fitness influencer endorsing a product says nothing about its actual efficacy unless their expertise matches the specific claim being made.

questions.stem: "A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. Therefore, a feather cannot be dark." The flaw here is:

options.text: Equivocation — "light" shifts meaning between "not heavy" and "bright/pale in colour" across the argument.
A false dilemma.
An ad hominem.
A hasty generalisation.

questions.explanation: The word "light" means "not heavy" in the first premise but is treated as "bright in colour" in the second — a hidden shift in meaning that makes the argument only look valid.
questions.principle_title: Equivocation: one word, two meanings
questions.principle_explanation: Equivocation fallacies exploit a word with multiple meanings, using one meaning in one premise and a different meaning elsewhere, so the argument appears to connect logically when it doesn't. Always check that key terms mean the same thing every time they're used.
questions.memory_tip: "One word, two hats": equivocation happens when a word quietly swaps meanings mid-argument. Re-read the argument substituting one fixed meaning for the key word every time, and watch it fall apart.
questions.real_world_application: Legal and contract disputes often hinge on equivocation — a word like "reasonable" or "material" quietly shifting meaning between clauses. Courts spend enormous effort pinning down a single consistent meaning for exactly this reason.

questions.stem: A report states: "Unemployment fell from 6% to 5% this year, while the number of people actively looking for work also fell." What is the most cautious interpretation?

options.text: The economy has definitely improved and created many new jobs.
The fall in the unemployment rate might partly reflect people leaving the labour force (giving up looking), not only new employment.
The unemployment rate is meaningless.
The data must be incorrect since both numbers fell together.

questions.explanation: Unemployment rate = (people looking for work but without a job) ÷ (people in the labour force). If people stop looking for work, they leave the denominator too, which can lower the rate without any new jobs being created.
questions.principle_title: Reading behind a single statistic
questions.principle_explanation: A rate is a ratio — always ask what is in the numerator and denominator, and what could move each of them. A statistic can improve for reasons that don't match the story being told about it.
questions.memory_tip: "Top and bottom": a rate is a fraction. Before trusting any "the rate went up/down" claim, ask what moved on top (the numerator) and what moved on the bottom (the denominator).
questions.real_world_application: This is the exact reasoning error behind many "crime is falling" or "unemployment improved" headlines — the underlying ratio can shift for reasons that have nothing to do with the story being told. Journalists and policy analysts who skip this check regularly publish misleading conclusions.

questions.stem: "Some argue that remote work harms company culture. But teams that meet in person quarterly report just as strong a sense of belonging as fully office-based teams." What is the function of the second sentence?

options.text: It restates the counterargument without addressing it.
It presents evidence that rebuts the counterargument mentioned in the first sentence.
It introduces an unrelated new topic.
It is an ad hominem against remote workers.

questions.explanation: The passage first raises an opposing view (remote work harms culture), then immediately offers evidence against it — a rebuttal structure common in persuasive writing.
questions.principle_title: Spotting concession-and-rebuttal structure
questions.principle_explanation: Strong persuasive writing often raises the other side's best point (concession) before countering it (rebuttal). Recognising this structure helps you separate what the author actually believes from the objection they're temporarily voicing.
questions.memory_tip: Listen for "yes... but": strong persuasive writing often concedes the other side's best point first ("yes, I hear that...") before pivoting to the rebuttal ("...but here's why"). The "but" is your cue.
questions.real_world_application: This is the backbone of persuasive essay writing (including GAMSAT Section II) and of any strong opinion piece: acknowledge the best opposing point before showing why your position still holds, which is far more convincing than ignoring the other side entirely.

questions.topic: Tone and Irony in Literary Excerpts
questions.stem: "He wore his humility like a medal, polished daily, displayed to anyone who would look." The literary device at work here is best described as:

options.text: A sincere compliment about the subject's modesty.
Paradox/irony — describing "humility" in terms of vanity (a medal, polished, displayed) to suggest the humility is actually performative.
A literal description of a military award.
Onomatopoeia.

questions.explanation: Genuine humility isn't "displayed" or "polished" for an audience — describing it that way turns the compliment into a critique of the subject's self-regard.
questions.principle_title: Reading literary irony
questions.principle_explanation: When a text describes a virtue using the imagery of its opposite (humility as vanity, generosity as showing off), it is usually signalling irony or critique, not sincerity. Look for a mismatch between the label used and the imagery surrounding it.
questions.memory_tip: Label vs picture: when the label on a virtue ("humility") doesn't match the picture painted around it (medals, polish, display), trust the picture — that mismatch is the irony.
questions.real_world_application: This is how satire and literary criticism work — a writer describing a corrupt politician's "integrity" in glowing, exaggerated terms to mock rather than praise them. Missing the irony means completely misreading the author's actual point.

questions.stem: Claim: "This new medication is effective." Which piece of evidence would most strongly support this claim?

options.text: A testimonial from one patient who felt better after taking it.
A large randomised controlled trial showing significantly better outcomes than a placebo group.
The manufacturer's marketing brochure.
The fact that the medication has an official-sounding name.

questions.explanation: Randomisation and a placebo control group rule out bias and the placebo effect, and a large sample size makes the result statistically reliable — the gold standard for causal claims about treatment effectiveness.
questions.principle_title: Ranking evidence quality
questions.principle_explanation: Not all evidence is equal. Anecdote < uncontrolled observation < controlled study < large randomised controlled trial, roughly speaking. GAMSAT reasoning questions often ask you to rank or select the strongest available evidence for a claim.
questions.memory_tip: The AOCR ladder, weakest to strongest: Anecdote, Observation, Controlled study, Randomised trial. GAMSAT usually wants you standing on the top rung.
questions.real_world_application: This ranking is exactly what underlies evidence-based medicine: a single patient testimonial for a new treatment carries far less weight than a large randomised controlled trial, which is why regulators rely on the latter before approving anything.

questions.stem: "If the bridge is not repaired, the town will be cut off during floods. The bridge was repaired. Therefore, the town will not be cut off during floods." This argument is:

options.text: Valid, because it correctly negates both the condition and the consequence.
Invalid — this is "denying the antecedent"; repairing the bridge removes one risk but other causes of being cut off (e.g. landslides, road closures) may remain.
Valid, because bridges prevent all flooding.
Invalid, because the original conditional statement is false.

questions.explanation: The original statement only tells us what happens if the bridge is NOT repaired; it says nothing about what guarantees safety once it is repaired. Other causes of being cut off could still exist.
questions.principle_title: Denying the antecedent
questions.principle_explanation: From "if A then B," you cannot validly conclude "if not-A then not-B." The conditional only tells you about the presence of A, not what happens in its absence — a very common invalid pattern in GAMSAT-style arguments.
questions.memory_tip: "Fixing one door doesn't lock the whole house": repairing the bridge closes one named route to disaster, but other doors (other causes) may still be open. Never assume removing one stated cause removes every cause.
questions.real_world_application: Public safety messaging often implies this fallacy without meaning to — "wear a seatbelt or you'll die in a crash" doesn't mean wearing one guarantees safety, since other risks still exist. Good risk communication has to avoid implying false guarantees.

questions.stem: Which organelle is primarily responsible for producing the ATP a cell uses for energy?

options.text: Nucleus
Mitochondrion
Golgi apparatus
Ribosome

questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic (cellular) respiration, converting glucose and oxygen into ATP, the cell's usable energy currency.
questions.principle_title: Cells as tiny factories with specialised organelles
questions.principle_explanation: Each organelle has one main job: the nucleus stores DNA/instructions, mitochondria make energy (ATP), ribosomes build proteins, and the Golgi apparatus packages/ships molecules. Memorise organelle = job, not just organelle = definition.
questions.memory_tip: "Mitochondria = the powerhouse of the cell" is drilled in for a reason — say it out loud. Extend the same trick to the others: organelle = job title (nucleus = control room, ribosome = protein factory, Golgi = packaging/shipping department).
questions.real_world_application: This is why mitochondrial diseases (faults in the organelle that makes ATP) cause fatigue and muscle weakness across totally different body systems — everything that needs energy is affected, a direct real-world consequence of "mitochondria = the cell's power supply".

questions.stem: During protein synthesis, mRNA is translated into a chain of amino acids. What is this chain called before it folds into its final shape?

options.text: A polypeptide
A nucleotide
A codon
A ribosome

questions.explanation: Ribosomes read mRNA in three-letter codons, each specifying one amino acid; the amino acids link together into a polypeptide chain, which then folds into a functional protein.
questions.principle_title: DNA → RNA → protein (the central dogma)
questions.principle_explanation: DNA is transcribed into mRNA (in the nucleus), and mRNA is translated into protein (at ribosomes). A "codon" is a 3-letter code word in mRNA; a "polypeptide" is the resulting chain of amino acids before folding. Keep the sequence straight: transcription then translation.
questions.memory_tip: "Transcription in, Translation out": DNA is transcribed into mRNA inside the nucleus, then mRNA is translated into protein at the ribosome. Alphabetically, Transcription comes before Translation — same order it happens in the cell.
questions.real_world_application: This pathway is exactly what mRNA vaccines (like the COVID-19 vaccines) exploit — they deliver a synthetic mRNA instructing your own ribosomes to build a viral protein, triggering an immune response without ever touching your DNA.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes mitosis from meiosis?

options.text: Mitosis produces 4 genetically identical daughter cells; meiosis produces 2.
Mitosis produces 2 genetically identical diploid cells for growth/repair; meiosis produces 4 genetically varied haploid cells for reproduction.
Mitosis only occurs in plants; meiosis only occurs in animals.
Mitosis and meiosis produce identical outcomes but at different speeds.

questions.explanation: Mitosis is one division producing 2 identical diploid cells (growth, repair). Meiosis is two divisions producing 4 genetically distinct haploid gametes, halving chromosome number for sexual reproduction.
questions.principle_title: Mitosis = copies for the body; meiosis = gametes for reproduction
questions.principle_explanation: Anchor the purpose first: mitosis keeps your body growing and repaired with identical cells; meiosis creates sperm/egg cells with half the chromosome number and genetic variation (via crossing-over), so offspring differ from parents.
questions.memory_tip: Mitosis = "making more of me" (2 identical cells, for growth/repair). MeIosIs = the extra I's can remind you of "eggs" — it makes 4 different, half-DNA gametes for reproduction.
questions.real_world_application: Cancer is fundamentally a mitosis-control problem (cells dividing when they shouldn't), while IVF and genetic counselling are built on understanding meiosis — why egg and sperm cells carry only half the genetic material, and what can go wrong when they don't.

questions.stem: A particular enzyme works best at 37°C and pH 7. At 60°C, the enzyme stops working entirely, even after cooling back down. Why?

options.text: The enzyme has run out of substrate.
High heat denatured the enzyme, permanently disrupting its 3D shape (including the active site).
The enzyme was used up in the reaction.
The pH also changed at higher temperatures.

questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins whose function depends on a precise 3D shape, especially the active site. Excess heat breaks the bonds holding that shape together (denaturation), which is generally irreversible.
questions.principle_title: Enzymes are shape-dependent, reusable catalysts
questions.principle_explanation: Enzymes speed up reactions by binding substrates at an active site whose shape must fit precisely (like a lock and key/induced fit). Denaturation from heat or extreme pH permanently changes that shape, destroying function — this is different from simply "running out" of enzyme.
questions.memory_tip: Picture an enzyme as a wax figure left in the sun: overheat it and it melts out of shape permanently, even after it cools back down. That melted shape is denaturation — not the enzyme being "used up."
questions.real_world_application: This is why cooking an egg is irreversible, why a fever above about 41°C is medically dangerous (it starts denaturing your own enzymes), and why enzyme-based laundry detergents specify a maximum wash temperature on the label.

questions.stem: A red blood cell is placed in a hypotonic solution (lower solute concentration than inside the cell). What happens?

options.text: Water leaves the cell, and it shrivels.
Water enters the cell, and it may swell or burst.
No water moves because the cell membrane is impermeable to water.
Solutes leave the cell to balance concentrations.

questions.explanation: Osmosis moves water from an area of lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration across a semi-permeable membrane. In a hypotonic (more dilute) solution, water flows into the cell, which can cause it to swell or lyse.
questions.principle_title: Osmosis follows water toward higher solute concentration
questions.principle_explanation: Water moves to dilute the more concentrated side. Hypotonic outside = water rushes in (cell swells). Hypertonic outside = water rushes out (cell shrinks). Isotonic = no net movement. This single rule covers most osmosis questions.
questions.memory_tip: "Water follows the crowd": water always moves toward the side with more dissolved solute (the crowded side) to dilute it. Hypotonic outside = fewer solutes outside = water rushes IN and the cell swells.
questions.real_world_application: This is why doctors use isotonic saline (not plain water) for IV drips — infusing pure water would make red blood cells swell and burst by osmosis — and why sports drinks are formulated close to isotonic to avoid stomach discomfort.

questions.stem: In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant over white flowers (p). A heterozygous purple plant (Pp) is crossed with a white plant (pp). What fraction of offspring are expected to have white flowers?
questions.explanation: Pp × pp gives offspring genotypes Pp, Pp, pp, pp (1:1 ratio). Only pp is white, so 2 out of 4 = 1/2 are expected to be white.
questions.principle_title: Punnett squares and dominant/recessive alleles
questions.principle_explanation: A dominant allele (capital letter) masks a recessive allele (lowercase) in a heterozygote. Draw a 2x2 Punnett square, cross each parent's alleles, and count genotypes to find phenotype ratios. Pp x pp is a classic "test cross" pattern worth memorising.
questions.memory_tip: Always draw the Punnett square, even for "easy" ones — capital letter wins (dominant), lowercase only shows when paired with itself (recessive). Memorise "Pp x pp" as the classic test-cross template worth recognising on sight.
questions.real_world_application: This is the exact reasoning behind genetic counselling for conditions like cystic fibrosis: if both parents are carriers (heterozygous) of a recessive allele, a Punnett square shows a 1 in 4 chance of any child being affected.

questions.stem: A population of beetles has varying shell colour. After a change in habitat that increases visibility to predators, darker beetles start being eaten more often. Over many generations, which outcome does natural selection predict?

options.text: The beetles will consciously evolve to change colour within their own lifetime.
Lighter-coloured beetles will become more common, because they survive and reproduce more successfully in the new environment.
All beetles will die out immediately.
Colour has no effect on survival, since colour is random.

questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on existing variation: individuals whose traits improve survival and reproduction (here, lighter colour, better camouflage) leave more offspring, so that trait becomes more frequent in the population over generations — not within one individual's lifetime.
questions.principle_title: Natural selection acts on populations, not individuals
questions.principle_explanation: No individual organism "evolves" during its own life. Selection changes the frequency of traits across a population over generations, because individuals with advantageous variations survive/reproduce more. Variation must already exist for selection to act on it.
questions.memory_tip: "Survival of the fittest population, not the fittest individual's lifetime": no single beetle chooses to lighten up. The population's average colour shifts over generations because lighter beetles out-survive and out-reproduce darker ones.
questions.real_world_application: Antibiotic resistance is natural selection happening in real time: bacteria with a mutation that survives an antibiotic reproduce more, and over generations the resistant strain dominates — no individual bacterium "adapted", the population's makeup shifted.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches the general inputs and outputs of photosynthesis?

options.text: Inputs: glucose + oxygen. Outputs: carbon dioxide + water + energy.
Inputs: carbon dioxide + water + light energy. Outputs: glucose + oxygen.
Inputs: nitrogen + water. Outputs: glucose + carbon dioxide.
Inputs: glucose + water. Outputs: carbon dioxide + oxygen.

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis (in chloroplasts) uses light energy to convert CO2 and water into glucose and oxygen. This is essentially the reverse of cellular respiration, which breaks glucose + oxygen back down into CO2 + water + usable energy (ATP).
questions.principle_title: Photosynthesis and respiration are mirror-image processes
questions.principle_explanation: Photosynthesis (plants, using sunlight) builds glucose from CO2 + water, releasing oxygen. Cellular respiration (all living cells, including plants) breaks glucose back down using oxygen, releasing CO2, water and ATP. Learn them as reverses of each other and you'll never mix up inputs/outputs again.
questions.memory_tip: Mirror image: photosynthesis and respiration are exact opposites. Learn one equation and flip the arrow to get the other — CO2 + water + light -> glucose + oxygen, reversed, is glucose + oxygen -> CO2 + water + energy.
questions.real_world_application: This mirror relationship is the whole basis of how a sealed terrarium or the global carbon cycle stays roughly in balance — plants pulling in the CO2 that animals and decomposers breathe out, and vice versa for oxygen.

questions.stem: After a meal, blood glucose rises. Insulin is released, causing cells to take up glucose and lowering blood sugar back toward normal. This is an example of:

options.text: Positive feedback, amplifying the original change.
Negative feedback, counteracting the original change to restore a stable set point.
A one-way, non-regulated process.
An immune response.

questions.explanation: The rise in glucose triggers a response (insulin release) that pushes glucose back down — the response opposes the original change, which is the hallmark of negative feedback.
questions.principle_title: Negative feedback maintains stable internal conditions
questions.principle_explanation: Most homeostatic systems (blood sugar, body temperature, blood pressure) use negative feedback: a deviation from the set point triggers a corrective response in the opposite direction. Positive feedback (e.g. childbirth contractions, blood clotting) instead amplifies change — much rarer in the body.
questions.memory_tip: Thermostat rule: negative feedback works like a thermostat correcting back toward a set point (blood sugar too high -> insulin brings it down). Positive feedback is the rare exception that amplifies change, like a snowball rolling downhill (e.g. childbirth contractions).
questions.real_world_application: This is literally how a home thermostat and your own body temperature regulation both work, and it's why diabetes (a breakdown in the insulin negative-feedback loop) causes blood sugar to swing out of control instead of self-correcting.

questions.stem: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygenated blood out to the rest of the body?

options.text: Right atrium
Right ventricle
Left atrium
Left ventricle

questions.explanation: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium, passes into the left ventricle, which is the most muscular chamber and pumps blood at high pressure out through the aorta to the whole body.
questions.principle_title: Right heart = lungs, left heart = body
questions.principle_explanation: Simplify the heart into two pumps in series: the right side receives deoxygenated blood from the body and sends it to the lungs; the left side receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and sends it to the body. The left ventricle is thickest because it pumps against the greatest resistance (the whole body).
questions.memory_tip: "Right to lungs, left to limbs": the right side of the heart sends blood on a short trip to the lungs; the thicker, stronger left side pumps it the long way round the whole body.
questions.real_world_application: This is why a "left-sided" heart attack (affecting the more muscular left ventricle) is typically far more dangerous than damage to the right side — the left ventricle does the harder job of pumping blood around the entire body.

questions.stem: Antibodies are produced by which type of cell?

options.text: Red blood cells
B lymphocytes (B cells)
Platelets
Neurons

questions.explanation: B cells, once activated, differentiate into plasma cells that produce and secrete antibodies specific to a particular antigen.
questions.principle_title: Adaptive immunity: B cells vs T cells
questions.principle_explanation: The adaptive immune system's two main lymphocyte types have different jobs: B cells produce antibodies (the "humoral" response, tagging pathogens for destruction), while T cells directly kill infected cells or help coordinate the immune response. Antibody = B cell is a very testable fact.
questions.memory_tip: "B is for antiBody" — B cells make antiBodies (both start with B). T cells are the ones that Touch and kill infected cells directly.
questions.real_world_application: This distinction underlies different vaccine types and immune therapies — some vaccines are designed to trigger strong antibody (B cell) responses, while some cancer immunotherapies instead unleash T cells to directly kill tumour cells.

questions.stem: Hormones typically travel through the body and reach their target via which route?

options.text: Directly through nerve synapses only
The bloodstream, acting on target cells with matching receptors anywhere in the body
Only through the digestive tract
Only by direct cell-to-cell contact

questions.explanation: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood; they travel throughout the body but only affect cells that have the matching receptor for that hormone.
questions.principle_title: Hormones = slow, broadcast signals; nerves = fast, direct signals
questions.principle_explanation: Compare the two communication systems: the nervous system sends fast, short-lived electrical signals to specific target cells via synapses; the endocrine system sends slower, longer-lasting chemical signals (hormones) broadcast through the blood, acting only where matching receptors exist.
questions.memory_tip: Nerves = text message (fast, direct, to one specific person). Hormones = radio broadcast (slower, goes out to everyone, only picked up by those tuned to the right receptor/frequency).
questions.real_world_application: This is why a reflex (nervous system) happens in milliseconds but puberty or the stress response (hormonal/endocrine system) unfolds over minutes, days or years — fast direct wiring versus a slow broadcast signal.

questions.stem: An atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons, and is neutral. How many electrons does it have?
questions.explanation: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. Protons = 17, so electrons = 17 (neutrons don't affect charge or electron count).
questions.principle_title: Protons define the element; electrons balance charge
questions.principle_explanation: Protons (positive) determine which element an atom is and its atomic number. In a neutral atom, electrons (negative) equal protons to balance charge. Neutrons add mass but no charge, and don't affect electron count. Ions are just atoms that gained/lost electrons, so protons ≠ electrons.
questions.memory_tip: Protons are your passport — they define your identity (the element) and never change without you becoming a different element. Electrons just balance the books to keep a neutral atom's charge at zero.
questions.real_world_application: This is the basis of isotopes used in medicine — carbon-14 dating and PET-scan tracers work by varying the neutron count (changing atomic mass) while keeping the proton count, and therefore the element's chemistry, identical.

questions.stem: Moving left to right across a period (row) of the periodic table, atomic radius generally:

options.text: Increases, because more electrons take up more space.
Decreases, because increasing nuclear charge pulls the same electron shell in more tightly.
Stays exactly the same.
Changes randomly with no pattern.

questions.explanation: Across a period, electrons are added to the same outer shell while protons (and thus positive nuclear charge) also increase. The stronger pull draws the electron cloud in closer, shrinking atomic radius.
questions.principle_title: Periodic trends come from nuclear charge vs shielding
questions.principle_explanation: Across a period: more protons pull the same shell in tighter -> radius shrinks, ionisation energy rises. Down a group: an extra electron shell is added each row, with inner electrons shielding the pull -> radius grows, ionisation energy falls. Learn the "why" (charge vs shielding) rather than memorising each trend separately.
questions.memory_tip: Picture the nucleus in a tug of war with its electrons: across a period, more protons pull the SAME shell in tighter (radius shrinks); down a group, a whole new outer shell is added each row, further from the pull (radius grows).
questions.real_world_application: This is why sodium (large atom, low ionisation energy, loses its outer electron easily) reacts explosively with water while a small, tightly-bound atom like fluorine behaves completely differently — periodic trends predict reactivity patterns chemists rely on daily.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride (NaCl) and water (H2O) are both compounds, but they bond very differently. Why?

options.text: NaCl forms ionic bonds (metal + non-metal, electron transfer); water forms covalent bonds (non-metal + non-metal, electron sharing).
Both form identical bond types, but at different temperatures.
NaCl shares electrons; water transfers them completely.
Bond type depends only on molecular size.

questions.explanation: Sodium (a metal) transfers an electron to chlorine (a non-metal), forming oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction (ionic bond). In water, two hydrogen atoms share electrons with oxygen (covalent bonds) since both are non-metals.
questions.principle_title: Metal + non-metal = ionic; non-metal + non-metal = covalent
questions.principle_explanation: As a rule of thumb: ionic bonds form when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal, creating charged ions that attract. Covalent bonds form when two non-metals share electron pairs. This single rule predicts bond type for most GAMSAT-level compounds.
questions.memory_tip: "Metals give, non-metals share": a metal + non-metal pairing means one atom GIVES away an electron (ionic bond); two non-metals SHARE electrons because neither wants to give theirs up (covalent bond).
questions.real_world_application: This is why table salt (ionic NaCl) dissolves in water and conducts electricity as a solution, while sugar (covalent, molecular) dissolves but doesn't conduct — bond type predicts real, testable everyday behaviour.

questions.stem: Balance this equation and state the coefficient in front of O2: __ CH4 + __ O2 -> __ CO2 + __ H2O
questions.explanation: 1 C and 4 H on the left need 1 CO2 and 2 H2O on the right, which together contain 2+2 = 4 oxygen atoms, requiring 2 O2 molecules on the left.
questions.principle_title: Balancing equations = conservation of atoms
questions.principle_explanation: Chemical equations must have the same number of each type of atom on both sides (atoms are neither created nor destroyed). Balance one element at a time, usually leaving oxygen for last since it often appears in multiple products.
questions.memory_tip: "Atoms are never created or destroyed, only rearranged" — balance one element at a time and save oxygen for last, since it tends to show up on both sides of the equation.
questions.real_world_application: This is exactly the calculation behind industrial processes like the Haber process for fertiliser production, where getting the stoichiometric ratios right determines how much ammonia — and ultimately food supply — a plant can produce from a given amount of raw gas.

questions.stem: A solution has a pH of 3. Compared to a solution with pH 5, the pH 3 solution is:

options.text: Less acidic, with a lower H+ concentration
More acidic, with 100 times higher H+ concentration
More acidic, with only 2 times higher H+ concentration
Basic, not acidic

questions.explanation: pH is a log scale: pH = -log10[H+]. Each whole-number drop in pH means a 10-fold increase in H+ concentration. Going from pH 5 to pH 3 is a difference of 2, so H+ concentration is 10^2 = 100 times higher.
questions.principle_title: pH is logarithmic, not linear
questions.principle_explanation: A common trap: assuming pH differences are linear. Because pH is a log10 scale of H+ concentration, every 1-unit drop means 10x more H+ ions (more acidic), and every 1-unit rise means 10x fewer (more basic/alkaline).
questions.memory_tip: "Every step is a 10x leap": pH is a log scale, so each single-unit drop means 10x more H+. Count the gap between the two pH numbers, then raise 10 to that power.
questions.real_world_application: This is why "mildly acidic" rain at pH 4 is actually 100 times more acidic than normal rain at pH 6, and why swimming pool pH is tightly controlled — small pH-number changes represent huge changes in actual acidity.

questions.stem: In the reaction Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, which species is oxidised?

options.text: Zn, because it loses electrons and its charge increases from 0 to +2
Cu2+, because it gains electrons
Both are reduced
Neither, since no electrons are transferred

questions.explanation: Zn goes from a neutral charge (0) to +2, meaning it lost two electrons — oxidation. Cu2+ goes from +2 to 0, gaining two electrons — reduction. Electrons lost by Zn are gained by Cu2+.
questions.principle_title: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons)
questions.principle_explanation: Track charge changes to identify redox: if an atom's oxidation state increases, it lost electrons (oxidised). If it decreases, it gained electrons (reduced). The mnemonic "OIL RIG" (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain) is one of the most reliable shortcuts on the whole test.
questions.memory_tip: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). Say it out loud until it sticks; it solves almost every redox question on its own.
questions.real_world_application: This is the chemistry behind batteries (redox reactions generating an electric current) and behind rusting, where iron is slowly oxidised — anywhere electrons move between substances, redox and OIL RIG apply.

questions.stem: A fixed amount of gas is heated at constant volume. What happens to its pressure, and why?

options.text: Pressure decreases, because heat makes gas particles slower.
Pressure increases, because faster-moving particles collide with the container walls more frequently and forcefully.
Pressure stays the same, since volume is fixed.
The gas turns to liquid.

questions.explanation: Heating increases the average kinetic energy (speed) of gas particles. At constant volume, faster particles hit the container walls harder and more often, increasing pressure — consistent with Gay-Lussac's Law (P proportional to T at constant V).
questions.principle_title: Kinetic theory links temperature, pressure and volume
questions.principle_explanation: Think of gas laws through particle motion, not just formulas: temperature reflects average particle speed; pressure comes from particles colliding with walls. Raise temperature at fixed volume -> more forceful/frequent collisions -> higher pressure. This intuition covers Boyle's, Charles's and Gay-Lussac's laws.
questions.memory_tip: Picture gas particles as tiny tennis balls bouncing off the container walls: heat them up and they slam the walls faster and more often — "faster particles hit harder," which is why pressure rises.
questions.real_world_application: This is why a sealed can of deodorant can explode if left in a hot car — heating the gas at fixed volume increases pressure until the container fails — and why tyre pressure needs checking more carefully in extreme temperature swings.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.5 moles of NaCl in 250 mL of water?
questions.explanation: Molarity = moles of solute / litres of solution = 0.5 mol / 0.25 L = 2 mol/L.
questions.principle_title: Molarity = moles per litre
questions.principle_explanation: Always convert volume to litres before dividing. Molarity (M) = mol of solute ÷ L of solution. This single formula, rearranged, solves the majority of GAMSAT concentration/dilution questions.
questions.memory_tip: "M is for moles-per-litre": Molarity = moles over litres. Always convert mL to L (divide by 1000) before you divide, every single time.
questions.real_world_application: Every pharmacy dose and IV drip calculation ultimately comes down to molarity — getting the moles-per-litre wrong when diluting a medication is a real and dangerous clinical error, which is exactly why the concept is drilled so hard.

questions.stem: For the equilibrium N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3 (exothermic forward reaction), what happens if the temperature is increased?

options.text: The equilibrium shifts toward the products (more NH3) to absorb the extra heat.
The equilibrium shifts toward the reactants (less NH3), since the reverse (endothermic) reaction is favoured to absorb the added heat.
Nothing changes; equilibrium is unaffected by temperature.
The reaction stops completely.

questions.explanation: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium shifts to counteract an applied change. Adding heat is treated like adding a "product" of the endothermic (reverse) direction, so the equilibrium shifts toward the reactants, favouring the reverse (heat-absorbing) reaction.
questions.principle_title: Le Chatelier's principle: systems counteract change
questions.principle_explanation: When you stress an equilibrium (change in concentration, pressure/volume, or temperature), the reaction shifts in the direction that partially opposes that stress. For temperature specifically, treat heat like a reactant/product: increasing heat favours whichever direction absorbs heat (the endothermic direction).
questions.memory_tip: "The system pushes back": treat added heat like an extra ingredient on whichever side absorbs it (the endothermic direction), and picture the equilibrium physically leaning away from the stress you applied.
questions.real_world_application: Industrial ammonia production (the Haber process again) is deliberately run at carefully chosen temperature and pressure specifically to push the Le Chatelier equilibrium toward more product — this one principle underlies a huge chunk of industrial chemistry.

questions.stem: A molecule contains a -COOH group. What functional group is this, and what general property does it give the molecule?

options.text: An alcohol group; makes the molecule strongly basic
A carboxylic acid group; makes the molecule acidic (can donate a H+)
An amine group; makes the molecule non-reactive
A ketone group; has no acidic or basic properties

questions.explanation: -COOH is the carboxylic acid functional group. It can donate the hydrogen from -OH as H+, making carboxylic-acid-containing molecules (like acetic acid, amino acids) mildly acidic.
questions.principle_title: Functional groups predict chemical behaviour
questions.principle_explanation: In organic chemistry, a molecule's reactivity is largely determined by its functional groups, not its overall size. Recognise a handful of common ones: -OH (alcohol), -COOH (carboxylic acid, acidic), -NH2 (amine, basic), C=O (ketone/aldehyde). GAMSAT tests pattern recognition here, not memorising every organic reaction.
questions.memory_tip: Functional groups are name tags telling you how a molecule behaves at a party: -COOH wears the "acidic" tag (carboxylic acid), -NH2 wears the "basic" tag (amine), -OH wears the "alcohol" tag. Learn the tag, not the whole molecule.
questions.real_world_application: This is why aspirin (which contains a carboxylic acid group) is mildly acidic and can irritate the stomach lining, while paracetamol (different functional groups) doesn't share that side effect — a molecule's functional groups predict real pharmacological behaviour.

questions.stem: Crushing a solid reactant into a fine powder before reacting it with an acid speeds up the reaction. Why?

options.text: Powdering changes the chemical identity of the solid.
Powdering increases the total surface area exposed to the acid, allowing more frequent collisions between reacting particles.
Powdering lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
Powdering increases the temperature of the mixture.

questions.explanation: Reaction rate depends on collision frequency between reactant particles. A powder has far more surface area exposed than a single lump of the same mass, so more particles are available to collide with acid particles per second.
questions.principle_title: Collision theory explains reaction rate factors
questions.principle_explanation: Reaction rate increases whenever particles collide more often or with more energy: higher concentration/pressure (more particles per volume), higher temperature (faster, more energetic particles), greater surface area (more exposed particles), or a catalyst (lowers activation energy, without being consumed).
questions.memory_tip: "Crushed ice melts faster than an ice cube": more surface area means more particles exposed and able to collide, which is exactly why powdering speeds up a reaction.
questions.real_world_application: This is why powdered sugar dissolves and burns faster than a sugar cube, and why crushed antacid tablets relieve heartburn faster than swallowing them whole — more surface area means more collisions means a faster reaction.

questions.stem: A reaction releases heat to its surroundings, and the surrounding temperature rises. This reaction is:

options.text: Endothermic, with positive enthalpy change (ΔH > 0)
Exothermic, with negative enthalpy change (ΔH < 0)
Neutral, with ΔH = 0
Impossible to classify without knowing the reactants

questions.explanation: Releasing heat to the surroundings means the system loses energy, so enthalpy decreases (ΔH is negative) — this defines an exothermic reaction.
questions.principle_title: Exothermic releases heat (ΔH<0); endothermic absorbs heat (ΔH>0)
questions.principle_explanation: Think from the system's point of view: if the system loses energy to the surroundings (surroundings get warmer), that's exothermic and ΔH is negative. If the system absorbs energy from the surroundings (surroundings get colder), that's endothermic and ΔH is positive.
questions.memory_tip: "EXO = EXIT": in an EXOthermic reaction, heat EXits the system into the surroundings (they warm up, ΔH negative). ENDOthermic instead pulls heat IN, cooling the surroundings.
questions.real_world_application: Instant cold packs (endothermic, absorbing heat) and instant hot packs (exothermic, releasing heat) used for sports injuries are direct real-world applications of this exact chemistry, triggered by breaking an internal pouch to start the reaction.

questions.stem: A book rests on a table, unmoving. According to Newton's first law, this means:

options.text: No forces are acting on the book at all.
The net force on the book is zero — gravity pulling down is exactly balanced by the table's normal force pushing up.
The book is accelerating very slowly.
Gravity has stopped acting on the book.

questions.explanation: Newton's first law: an object at rest stays at rest unless acted on by a net (unbalanced) force. Here, gravity and the table's normal (support) force are equal and opposite, so they cancel — net force is zero, hence no acceleration.
questions.principle_title: Newton's first law: zero net force means zero acceleration
questions.principle_explanation: An object being "at rest" doesn't mean no forces act on it — it means all the forces acting on it are balanced (sum to zero). Always look for the pairs of forces holding a stationary object in equilibrium, like weight vs normal force.
questions.memory_tip: "Balanced forces, not no forces": a book sitting still isn't force-free, it's a tug of war in a dead heat. Newton's first law is about the NET force being zero, not the absence of forces.
questions.real_world_application: This is why passengers lurch forward when a car brakes suddenly — their body obeys Newton's first law and keeps moving until a net force (the seatbelt) acts on it — the entire safety rationale behind seatbelts and airbags.

questions.stem: A 2 kg object experiences a net force of 10 N. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: F = ma, so a = F/m = 10 N / 2 kg = 5 m/s^2.
questions.principle_title: F = ma links force, mass and acceleration
questions.principle_explanation: Newton's second law says net force equals mass times acceleration. For a fixed force, heavier objects accelerate less; for a fixed mass, bigger forces cause more acceleration. Nearly every GAMSAT dynamics question is a rearrangement of this one equation.
questions.memory_tip: "Fat mama accelerates slowly": F = ma — more mass (m) needs more force (F) to reach the same acceleration (a). Rearrange freely, since GAMSAT will ask you to solve for any one of the three.
questions.real_world_application: This is the calculation behind vehicle safety ratings and crash design: for a given collision force, a lighter car experiences greater acceleration — and therefore greater potential injury — than a heavier one, part of why crumple zones and mass distribution matter.

questions.stem: A ball is dropped from a height and falls freely (ignoring air resistance). As it falls, what happens to its total mechanical energy?

options.text: It increases, because kinetic energy is being created from nothing.
It stays constant — gravitational potential energy converts into kinetic energy, but the total stays the same.
It decreases steadily to zero.
It is entirely converted to heat immediately.

questions.explanation: With no air resistance, no energy leaves the ball-Earth system. Potential energy (mgh) converts into kinetic energy (½mv²) as it falls, but the sum of the two remains constant — conservation of mechanical energy.
questions.principle_title: Conservation of energy: energy changes form, not amount
questions.principle_explanation: In a closed system with no friction/air resistance, total mechanical energy (potential + kinetic) is conserved — it just converts between forms. When friction or air resistance is present, some mechanical energy converts to heat, which is why real systems appear to "lose" energy.
questions.memory_tip: "Energy just changes outfits": in a frictionless system, energy never disappears, it just swaps from a potential "outfit" to a kinetic one and back, with the total wardrobe value unchanged.
questions.real_world_application: This is why a pendulum (or a rollercoaster) keeps swinging back to almost the same height each time, and why "almost" rather than "exactly" — a small amount of mechanical energy is lost to air resistance and friction as heat each cycle.

questions.stem: A circuit has a resistance of 4 ohms and a current of 3 amps flowing through it. What is the voltage across it?
questions.explanation: Ohm's law: V = IR = 3 A x 4 ohm = 12 V.
questions.principle_title: Ohm's law connects voltage, current and resistance
questions.principle_explanation: V = IR is the core relationship in circuit questions: voltage is the "push," current is the flow of charge, and resistance opposes that flow. Learn to rearrange it (I = V/R, R = V/I) since GAMSAT will ask for any of the three variables.
questions.memory_tip: V = I x R — picture voltage as the "push," current as the "flow," and resistance as the "squeeze." A bigger squeeze needs a bigger push to keep the same flow going.
questions.real_world_application: This is the calculation every electrician and appliance designer uses to make sure a circuit doesn't draw dangerous current — get V=IR wrong and you either underpower a device or risk overheating and fire.

questions.stem: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: Wave speed = frequency x wavelength = 5 Hz x 2 m = 10 m/s.
questions.principle_title: Wave speed = frequency x wavelength
questions.principle_explanation: This one equation (v = fλ) governs sound, light, and water waves alike. Frequency (waves per second) and wavelength (distance between wave peaks) trade off against each other for a wave of fixed speed — e.g. for light in a vacuum, higher frequency always means shorter wavelength.
questions.memory_tip: "Very fast lambdas": v = fλ — wave speed equals frequency times wavelength (lambda). For a fixed speed, frequency and wavelength see-saw against each other: one up, the other down.
questions.real_world_application: This is why a lightning flash and its thunder don't arrive together — light and sound both obey v=fλ but travel at vastly different speeds — and it's the same equation behind tuning a radio or a musical instrument.

questions.stem: The same force is applied over a smaller area versus a larger area. Where is the resulting pressure greater?

options.text: Pressure is greater when spread over the larger area.
Pressure is greater when concentrated on the smaller area, since pressure = force / area.
Pressure is identical regardless of area.
Pressure cannot be determined from force and area alone.

questions.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area. For the same force, a smaller area gives a larger pressure (this is why knives are sharpened to a thin edge, and snowshoes have a large area to reduce pressure on snow).
questions.principle_title: Pressure = force per unit area
questions.principle_explanation: The formula P = F/A explains a huge range of everyday phenomena: sharp objects concentrate force into tiny areas for high pressure (cutting), while wide bases (snowshoes, tank treads) spread force over large areas for low pressure. Keep force and pressure conceptually distinct.
questions.memory_tip: "Sharp = small area = high pressure": a knife concentrates force onto a tiny edge (cuts easily); snowshoes spread the same force over a big area (don't sink). Same force, different area, very different pressure.
questions.real_world_application: This is why a drawing pin has a wide flat head but a sharp point (concentrating your finger's force into a tiny area to pierce a surface), and why snowshoes and tank treads use the opposite trick — spreading force over a wide area to avoid sinking.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an assumption the author relies on but does not explicitly state?

options.text: Most celebrated individual achievements would have been impossible without prior or contemporaneous input from others.
Newton, Curie and the unnamed writer never contributed anything original of their own.
Biographies about lone geniuses are more commercially successful than accurate ones.
Historians of science are always correct about the individuals they study.

questions.explanation: The author's argument (that crediting one mind "erases the scaffolding") only works if that scaffolding was genuinely necessary to the achievement, not merely present alongside it. That link — between "input existed" and "the achievement depended on it" — is assumed rather than argued for.
questions.principle_title: Finding the unstated assumption in a persuasive passage
questions.principle_explanation: When a passage moves from "collaborators existed" to "the achievement depended on those collaborators," it is smuggling in an assumption about necessity, not just presence. Ask: what extra premise turns "X was around" into "X was essential"?
questions.memory_tip: Same rope-bridge trick as before: find the plank the argument needs but never lays down. Here the plank is "present = necessary" — the author never actually shows the scaffolding was load-bearing, just that it existed.
questions.real_world_application: This is exactly how patent and Nobel Prize disputes get litigated — courts and prize committees regularly have to decide whether a named contributor's input was merely present or genuinely necessary to a breakthrough, which is precisely the gap this question is testing.
questions.stimulus: For centuries we have told the story of the solitary genius: Newton alone under his apple tree, Curie alone in her laboratory, the writer alone at her desk producing a masterpiece from nothing but personal brilliance. To argue that individual credit for innovation often obscures the collective foundations that made it possible.
To provide a detailed biography of Isaac Newton's scientific career.
To argue that biographies should never be written about scientists.

A study finds that a significant proportion of major scientific breakthroughs were made by isolated individuals with no access to relevant prior work or contemporaries.
Curie won two Nobel Prizes in different scientific fields.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of using this report to claim that social media causes anxiety?

options.text: The report did not survey enough teenagers to be statistically meaningful.
The data shows an association at one point in time, and cannot rule out reverse causation or a shared underlying cause such as poor sleep.
Teenagers are unreliable narrators of their own emotional states.
Anxiety cannot be measured using a survey.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly raises two alternative explanations — reverse causation (anxious teens retreat into phones) and a shared cause (poor sleep driving both) — which cross-sectional, single-timepoint data cannot distinguish from social-media-causes-anxiety.
questions.principle_title: Cross-sectional data cannot establish causation or its direction
questions.principle_explanation: A snapshot taken at one moment can show that two things go together, but it cannot show which came first, or whether both are driven by a third factor. Longitudinal data (tracking the same people over time) is needed to start untangling direction and cause.
questions.memory_tip: Same puppeteer image, new stage: this time the puppeteer might be poor sleep, or the puppets might even be pulling each other's strings in reverse (anxiety causing phone use, not the other way around). A snapshot can't tell you which.
questions.real_world_application: This exact caveat shows up every time a headline claims a food, habit or product 'causes' a health outcome based on a single survey — distinguishing snapshot correlation from tracked causation is core to reading nutrition and public-health journalism critically.
questions.stimulus: A widely circulated report claims that teenagers who spend more than four hours a day on social media are twice as likely to report symptoms of anxiety as teenagers who spend less than one hour a day. Newspaper headlines quickly translated this into warnings that social media "causes" anxiety in teenagers, and several schools cited the report when introducing new phone bans. The original researchers were more cautious. They noted that their data was cross-sectional — collected at a single point in time — rather than following the same teenagers over years, and that anxious teenagers might simply be more likely to retreat into their phones, rather than phones making them anxious in the first place. They also noted that heavy social media use was more common among teenagers who already reported sleeping fewer than six hours a night, raising the possibility that disrupted sleep, not screen time itself, was doing much of the work.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what alternative explanation might account for the link between social media use and anxiety, other than social media directly causing it?
questions.correct_answer: Reduced/disrupted sleep (fewer than six hours a night) as a shared underlying cause of both heavier social media use and anxiety
questions.explanation: The passage states that heavy social media use was more common among teenagers already sleeping fewer than six hours a night, raising disrupted sleep as a plausible shared cause of both the social media use and the anxiety, rather than one directly causing the other.

questions.principle_explanation: A confound is a third factor that influences both variables being studied, creating the appearance of a direct link between them. Being able to name the specific confound — not just gesture at "other factors" — is what separates a strong answer from a vague one.

questions.real_world_application: Clinicians face this constantly: poor sleep, diet and social media use are all tangled together in a patient's life, and treating the wrong one as the "cause" wastes the limited time available for an actual intervention.

options.text: Surveying a larger number of teenagers at the same single point in time.
Following the same group of teenagers over several years, tracking both their social media use and anxiety levels as they change.
Asking teenagers to guess how anxious they think heavy social media users are.
Only surveying teenagers who do not use social media at all.

questions.explanation: A longitudinal design, following the same individuals over time, can show whether an increase in social media use precedes an increase in anxiety (supporting causation) rather than the two merely co-occurring, which is the key limitation a bigger one-off survey (A) would not fix.

questions.principle_explanation: Making a sample bigger only makes a snapshot more precise, not more informative about causation or timing. To test causation, you generally need to track the same subjects over time and see which change happens first.
questions.memory_tip: "Bigger snapshot, same blur": more people in a one-off survey doesn't sharpen the picture of what caused what — only watching the same people change over time does that.
